title: Iran's army chief orders Hormuz closed 'further day by day' as Qatar presses Washington
dek: Iran says three tankers under US escort hit mines, a claim nobody has confirmed; Qatar's prime minister met Rubio and Vance. A day earlier Tehran vowed 'every means' against the US blockade as the Treasury targeted its shadow banks.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Iran's army commander-in-chief has ordered the navy to keep tightening the closure of the Strait of Hormuz "further day by day" until Washington meets Tehran's seven conditions, as Qatar's prime minister pressed US leaders in Washington to bring the two sides back to talks. The order, by Major General Amir Hatami, came late on Monday, after Iran said it would use "every means" against the US naval blockade of its ports.

General Hatami said he was acting on the orders of the Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, and warned that if the United States started another war, Iran's response would be "without geographical limitation", according to reports. The parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who led Iran's delegation at the Islamabad talks, accused Washington of seeking a "neither-war-nor-peace" situation and said Iran would pursue "military ways to break the blockade", reports said.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three oil tankers suffered "powerful explosions and massive fires" after hitting mines on Monday, two of them while under US air escort. The Joint Maritime Information Centre, run by Western navies, said the mine claims were unconfirmed, and recorded 114 passages through the strait with US assistance between 19 and 21 November. US Central Command had not commented on the claims by Tuesday evening.

In Washington, Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, met Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President JD Vance on Monday. He said afterwards that the region "cannot bear a renewed escalation of tensions between the United States and Iran" and that Doha was working to bring both sides back to the table, reports said. Neither Washington nor Tehran announced any new talks. President Donald Trump said on Sunday that US strikes on Iran could resume after the New Year.

## Monday's exchanges

Iran said on Monday it would use "every means" to counter the United States' naval blockade of its ports, a day after President Donald Trump warned that Iranian ships trying to break it would be sent "to the bottom of the sea". Hours later the US Treasury imposed sanctions on 22 companies and eight people it said formed part of Iran's "shadow banking" network for oil payments.

"We will certainly not tolerate this situation and will use every means to counter US aggression," the foreign ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, told his weekly press briefing in Tehran, calling the blockade a violation of the UN Charter and "an act of crime", according to reports. Asked on Sunday about calls in Iran for a convoy of tankers to break the blockade, Mr Trump said: "I hope they do it; they'll all go down to the bottom of the sea, just like the rest of their navy."

## What Washington did

The Treasury said its action, the latest under what it calls Operation Economic Outcast, targeted exchange houses in Iran and front companies, most of them in Dubai and others in Hong Kong and Turkey, that it said process payments for Iranian oil, petrochemical and metals exporters. Among them is the Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold, which matches exporters earning foreign currency with importers, and a Dubai firm the Treasury said handled payments for the National Iranian Tanker Company. "Iran's shadow banking system is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in the release.

In a separate notice, the Treasury's financial crimes unit, FinCEN, said it had identified about $14.7 billion of financial activity between January 2025 and August 2026 potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking, with recipients in the United Arab Emirates receiving about 52 per cent. It said suspicious-activity reports are leads, not proof of wrongdoing. No India-based person or company was named in Monday's designations.

## The view from Tehran

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has said the Strait of Hormuz could reopen within hours once the other side meets its commitments. Mr Baghaei listed Iran's conditions as lifting US sanctions, ending the blockade and carrying out what Washington accepted under the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, reports said. Mr Trump has declared that memorandum void. Mr Baghaei spoke before Qatar's prime minister held his meetings in Washington.

## Claims at sea and on land

Iran's navy said several tankers had caught fire in the strait after striking mines; no maritime authority had confirmed this, and the claims could not be verified. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said on Sunday that military forces were involved in an incident with an oil tanker in the Gulf of Oman, without saying whose. US Central Command had not commented.

In Yemen, the Houthi movement said it had scored "a direct hit" on Saudi Arabia's Rabigh refinery on the Red Sea coast, home to the Petro Rabigh complex run with Japan's Sumitomo Chemical. The Saudi-led coalition's spokesman, Turki al-Malki, said air defences had "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile" fired towards the western region. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed any damage. The Red Sea coast matters more than usual now: Saudi Arabia has been moving crude by pipeline to its western ports to avoid Hormuz.

## Why it matters for India

India imports most of its crude oil and much of its gas, and a large share normally passes through Hormuz. An attack on the LPG tanker MT Tara Gas on 16 November left one Indian sailor missing. Monday's sanctions also matter for Indian shipping and trading firms that deal with Gulf traders, because doing business with a designated company can expose them to US penalties. Brent crude was trading near $89 a barrel late on Monday, down about 3 per cent on the day, according to market data. Indian markets were shut on Tuesday for Guru Nanak Jayanti, and New Delhi had made no statement on the latest exchanges by Tuesday evening.
